title: "Visualization"
format:
  html:

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| output: false
# code from prior sections
using CSV, DataFrames, PhyloNetworks, CairoMakie, PhyloMakie
using StatsBase, StatsModels, PhyloTraits
net = readnewick("data/polemonium_network_calibrated.phy");
for tip in net.node tip.name = replace(tip.name, r"_2$" => s""); end
traits = CSV.read("data/polemonium_traits_morph.csv", DataFrame)
subset!(traits, :morph => ByRow(in(tiplabels(net))))
dat = DataFrame(morph = String.(traits[:, :morph]),
                elevation = map( x -> (x .> 2.3 ? "hi" : "lo"), traits.elevation))
fit = fitdiscrete(net, :ERSM, dat.morph, select(dat, :elevation))
asr = ancestralreconstruction(fit)
```

Many visualizations are interesting, and they are essential for communication.
We give here a few examples.
For each example, we suggest that you go step by step and inspect each element
in the code. The more the code makes sense, the more we can customize it later
for our own needs on other data sets.

Each example below renders the network with `plot!` into a plain Makie `Axis`,
then composes native Makie primitives (`scatter!`, `text!`, `Makie.pie!`,
`Legend`) on top of it. `node_positions`/`edge_positions` read node and edge
coordinates directly off the rendered plot, so we never need to know a taxon's
position in advance.

## discrete trait data at the tips

Following the example of a [discrete](topic8-discrete.qmd) trait,
of high or low elevation, let's visualize the data at the tips.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-6-tips-discrete
#| fig-cap: "showing a discrete trait at the tips"
figure = Figure(size = (900, 500))
axis = Axis(figure[1, 1])
hidedecorations!(axis)
hidespines!(axis)
plot_handle = plot!(axis, net; tipoffset=0.5, xlim=(0.5, 16))

# query node/edge coordinates, to use for adding annotations on top
node_table = node_positions(plot_handle)  # info to add node annotations
edge_table = edge_positions(plot_handle)  # info to add edge annotations

# find order "o" in which species from data are listed in the network -- and in node_table
o = [findfirst(isequal(tax), dat.morph) for tax in tiplabels(net)]
dat.morph[o] == tiplabels(net) # should be true, if order o is as intended
tip_rows = filter(:isleaf => identity, node_table)
dat.morph[o] == tip_rows.name # should be true

# next: add grey & red points at the leaves
tip_col = map(x -> (x=="lo" ? :grey : :red), dat.elevation[o])
scatter!(axis, tip_rows.x .+ 0.1, tip_rows.y; color=tip_col, markersize=15)

# next: add a legend to say which color is for which state
Legend(
    figure[1, 2],
    [MarkerElement(color=c, marker=:circle, markersize=15) for c in (:red, :grey)],
    ["hi", "lo"];
    title="elevation",
)

# next: add γ's for gene flow edges
minor_hybrid_rows = filter(row -> row.ishybrid && !row.ismajor, edge_table)
text!(
    axis,
    minor_hybrid_rows.x .- 0.1,
    minor_hybrid_rows.y .+ 0.5 .* [-1, 1, 1];
    text = string.(round.(minor_hybrid_rows.gamma; digits=2)),
    color = :deepskyblue,
    fontsize = 12,
)

figure
```

## ancestral probabilities

Now let's go one step further and visualize the probabilities of "high"
and "low" elevation (as a binary trait) from
this [figure](topic8-discrete.qmd#fig-5-asr1)(b)
with pie charts instead of boring hard-to-read numbers.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-6-asr-discrete
#| fig-cap: "pie charts to show ancestral state probabilities"

colnames = names(asr)[3:end] # to get the correct state - probability match
# create a new column in the asr data frame, filled with the empty string ""
asr[!,:fake] .= ""; # to add fake internal node labels later: and extract their positions
asr # just to check

coltrait = (:red, :grey) # or anything else: a color Makie knows how to interpret

# start the plot
figure = Figure(size = (900, 500))
axis = Axis(figure[1, 1])
hidedecorations!(axis)
hidespines!(axis)
plot_handle = plot!(
    axis, fit.net;
    tipoffset=0.5, xlim=(0.5, 16), arrowlen=0.15,
    nodelabel = asr[:,[:nodenumber, :fake]],
)
node_table = node_positions(plot_handle) # had locations of internal nodes, this time

# add pie charts, using locations of internal nodes
for i in 1:nrow(asr) # loop over each row in the ancestral state reconstruction data frame
  ii = findfirst(isequal(asr[!,:nodenumber][i]), node_table.number)
  colpp = Vector(asr[i,colnames])
  Makie.pie!(
      axis,
      Makie.Point2f(node_table.x[ii], node_table.y[ii]),
      colpp;
      radius = 0.2,
      color = collect(coltrait),
  )
end
# add legend with correct mapping of color -> state
Legend(
    figure[1, 2],
    [PolyElement(color=c) for c in coltrait],
    colnames;
    title = "elevation",
)

figure
```

## continuous trait data at the tips

Here is an example to vizualize the actual elevation values,
at the tips.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-6-tips-continuous
#| fig-cap: "bar plot to visualize continuous traits at the tips. red: above average. grey: below average"
# plot the network with a large tip offset to leave space for bars
figure = Figure(size = (900, 550))
axis = Axis(figure[1, 1])
hidedecorations!(axis)
hidespines!(axis)
plot_handle = plot!(axis, net; tipoffset=2.2, xlim=(0.5, 17))
tip_rows = filter(:isleaf => identity, node_positions(plot_handle))

# create standardized version of elevation, such that 0 corresponds to the mean,
# and such that the range covers an interval of length 2:
# for the bars to fit between the tips and the taxon names
o = [findfirst(isequal(tax), traits.morph) for tax in tip_rows.name] # ordering
intervallength = 2
std_elev = intervallength .* standardize(UnitRangeTransform, traits.elevation[o])
std_elev .-= mean(std_elev) # now mean = 0, interval length still as desired
linecol = [(el < 0 ? :grey : :red) for el in std_elev] # grey if elevation < mean, red if elevation > mean
m = minimum(std_elev)    # new minimum elevation, after "standardization"
x0 = tip_rows.x[1] + 0.1 # x where the smallest bar should extend
xmean = x0 - m           # x where the mean value will go
# create the bars: linesegments! takes one flat vector of alternating
# (start, end) points, with one color per point
bar_points = Makie.Point2f[]
bar_colors = Symbol[]
for (elev, y, col) in zip(std_elev, tip_rows.y, linecol)
    push!(bar_points, Makie.Point2f(xmean, y))
    push!(bar_points, Makie.Point2f(xmean + elev, y))
    push!(bar_colors, col, col)
end
linesegments!(axis, bar_points; color = bar_colors, linewidth = 10)

# add a small reference scale to show the original min and max elevations.
# label positions are in data units (not a pixel offset), so Makie's
# automatic axis limits expand to include them rather than clipping them.
min_elev, max_elev = round.(extrema(traits.elevation[o]), digits=2)
scale_y = minimum(tip_rows.y) - 1.5
lines!(axis, [x0, x0 + intervallength], [scale_y, scale_y]; color = :black)
text!(
    axis,
    [x0, x0 + intervallength], fill(scale_y - 0.8, 2);
    text = string.([min_elev, max_elev]),
    align = (:center, :top),
)
text!(
    axis, x0 + intervallength / 2, scale_y - 1.8;
    text = "elevation (km)",
    align = (:center, :top),
)

figure
```


## ancestral state for a continuous trait

Let's change and look at log-leaflet area this time. We can use a color gradient
to visualize ancestral state reconstructions. The issue to keep in mind,
when reading such a visualization, and that we don't see confidence intervals,
and those tend to be wider and wider as we move back in time toward the root
(assuming data on extant taxa only).

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| warning: false
#| label: fig-6-asr-continuous
#| fig-cap: "prediction of mean log-leaflet area (not showing uncertainty)"

# fit the model, get ancestral state predictions
fit_larea = phylolm(@formula(larea ~ 1), traits, net, tipnames=:morph,
                    withinspecies_var=true, y_mean_std=true)
asr_larea = predict(ancestralreconstruction(fit_larea))
asr_larea[!,:fake] .= ""; # fake empty labels

# start the plot
figure = Figure(size = (950, 500))
axis = Axis(figure[1, 1])
hidedecorations!(axis)
hidespines!(axis)
plot_handle = plot!(
    axis, net;
    tipoffset=0.5, xlim=(0.5, 16),
    nodelabel = asr_larea[:,[:nodenumber, :fake]],
)
node_table = node_positions(plot_handle)

# find order to match tips between asr_larea and node_table
o = [findfirst(isequal(nn), asr_larea.nodenumber) for nn in node_table.number]
asr_larea.nodenumber[o] == node_table.number # should be true

# add the ancestral-state predictions as a continuous color gradient: no
# manual palette, binning, or R round-trip needed, Makie interpolates directly
scatter!(
    axis, node_table.x, node_table.y;
    color = asr_larea.prediction[o],
    colormap = :viridis,
    colorrange = extrema(asr_larea.prediction),
    markersize = 15,
)
Colorbar(
    figure[1, 2];
    colormap = :viridis,
    limits = extrema(asr_larea.prediction),
    label = "log-leaflet area",
)

figure
```
